claims.claim: Price is the exchange of something of value between a buyer and a seller; the value to the seller in a sale is referred to as price, and in plain terms price is the amount a customer pays for a product.
The price determines how much revenue a company will earn and drives the financial health of the organization; of the four Ps, price is the element through which revenue comes in.

The price-value equation is a subjective consumer assessment: value comes from comparing what the customer gets (quality) with what they pay, and price acts as an indicator of value to the buyer; price usually reflects perceived value rather than real value.

Cost-based pricing sets the price from the costs of doing business (cost plus a markup), and its biggest pitfall is that it may not align with customer value perception, risking overpricing or underpricing.
Competition-based pricing sets the price according to competitors' prices, and customer value-based pricing sets the price according to the value-added benefits customers perceive in the product.

The five critical Cs of pricing are cost, customers, channels of distribution, competition, and compatibility; cost alone cannot be the only basis for a pricing decision because buyers do not know or care what production costs.
All other factors being consistent, an increase in price results in a decrease in demand; the demand curve is the graph showing how quantity demanded changes with price, sloping down as price rises.

Prestige pricing sets high prices knowing that demand will increase with higher prices, because the higher price increases the perceived value of the product; the price-quality signal works as a cue when buyers cannot easily judge quality, but only when something supports the price.

Price skimming sets a high initial price for a new product and lowers it over time to attract customer segments in waves, while market penetration pricing sets the lowest possible initial price to gain as many customers as possible from the start.

Bundle pricing is a tactic that promotes purchasing multiple products at once, priced so the package costs less than buying the items separately; discounts are a core pricing decision, with companies analyzing when discounting is appropriate.

conflictingEvidence.note: Sources agree on the core relationship but frame it from different directions: OpenStax 12.3 presents cost-based, customer value-based, and competition-based as pricing objectives, while common practice names the same trio cost-plus, competitive, and value-based pricing; CFI corroborates the perceived-value framing of price. These are complementary framings of one set of approaches, not contradictions; the lesson names the approaches as cost-plus, competitive, and value-based and attributes the underlying objectives to OpenStax.

The demand curve states higher price means less demand, while prestige pricing states a higher price can raise demand. OpenStax presents both in the same section and frames prestige pricing as the strategy that negates the demand curve; the lesson keeps both and states the honest nuance (the signal needs support), so no contradiction is taught.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, 12.2 The Five Critical Cs of Pricing
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone text. Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: the five critical Cs of pricing — cost, customers, channels of distribution, competition, and compatibility; cost as the most obvious element but never the only basis for a price, because buyers do not know or care what production costs; and the need to price against what customers expect and are willing to pay and against competitors' offerings. Concepts adapted into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Marketing, 12.3 The Five-Step Procedure for Establishing Pricing Policy
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A backbone text. Fetched live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: the pricing objectives that map to the three named approaches — the customer value-based objective (price set according to the product's value-added benefits), the cost-based objective (price set from costs of doing business, with the pitfall that it may not align with customer value perception and can overprice or underprice), and the competition-based objective (price set according to competitors' prices); demand as the buyer's desire and willingness to purchase at various prices, with an increase in price resulting in a decrease in demand when all other factors are consistent; the demand curve as the graph of price versus quantity demanded; and prestige pricing, which sets high prices knowing demand can increase because the higher price raises perceived value. Concepts adapted into original prose.
